Finding: Tract 6.00 ranks first in vulnerability with a poverty rate of 63.7%, one of the highest in the county. Yet its obesity rate is only 31.9% and the ACS records no residents without a high school diploma. This is not a true exception to the education-obesity relationship. Tract 6.00 sits directly on the UNL campus. The poverty here reflects student incomes and graduate stipends rather than structural economic disadvantage. Every student cleared the high school diploma bar to enroll, which explains the 0%. The low obesity reflects the age profile of a student population, not resilience against poverty.
The adjacent tracts 18.00 and 19.00 show why this distinction matters. Both sit just below UNL and also have high poverty (56.7% and 55.3%), but they show obesity rates of 39.5% and 34.0%. These tracts capture the surrounding neighborhoods rather than the student population. The contrast between tract 6.00 and its neighbors illustrates a real limitation of tract level analysis. Poverty means something different depending on who is experiencing it, and the model cannot distinguish student poverty from structural poverty without additional demographic context.
Tract 4.00, ranked third, sits between campus and East Campus and likely contains a mix of student and non-student residents. Its 29.0% without a high school diploma, the highest in the county, signals substantial non-student population, and its 41.1% obesity rate shows that structural disadvantage is present regardless of the student composition.

Finding: Tract 7.00 sits directly east of the UNL campus. Its 16.6% without a high school diploma and high SNAP rate (16.3%) suggest real food insecurity, but the student-adjacent population keeps obesity at 33.0%. A younger age profile likely suppresses obesity regardless of economic stress as seen with tract 6.
Tract 10.02 is primarily commercial, consisting mainly of strips and restaurants. Its small residential population (low poverty at 9.4%, low SNAP at 2.8%) likely reflects a specific demographic living in a commercial corridor rather than a typical neighborhood. Educational disadvantage here does not come with the financial barriers that usually accompany it.
Both tracts reveal limitations of tract level analysis. Geographic and demographic context changes what the numbers mean, and the dominant education-obesity pattern likely holds better when populations are residentially stable in their neighborhoods.

Finding: Near grocery tracts average 36.4% obesity, higher than both moderate (33.7%) and far access (34.0%) tracts. This is counterintuitive but consistent with the broader analysis. Urban low-income tracts cluster near stores because cities are dense, but physical proximity does not determine affordability or food quality. The near grocery tier has an average poverty rate of 20.1% and SNAP rate of 12.3%, more than double the other tiers. Structural poverty drives the health outcomes regardless of how close a store is.

title: Vulnerability Ranking
text:
Income vs Health Outcomes
Poverty rate and median income both measure economic conditions but capture different things. Poverty is a threshold measure, counting residents below a fixed line. Median income measures the middle of the distribution. Comparing both against obesity shows whether the relationship holds regardless of which economic lens you use.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
ax.scatter(df_profiles['median_income'] / 1000, df_profiles['OBESITY_CrudePrev'], alpha=0.6, color='steelblue')
ax.set_xlabel('Median Income ($k)')
ax.set_ylabel('Obesity Rate (%)')
ax.set_title('Median Income vs Obesity Rate by Tract')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Finding: Median income shows a clear negative relationship with obesity across tracts. Higher income tracts cluster below 35% obesity while the highest obesity tracts tend to fall below $60k median income.
The relationship is not perfectly linear. Several low-income tracts have moderate obesity, consistent with the student population effects discussed earlier. The pattern reinforces the poverty rate finding that economic conditions predict health outcomes more reliably than physical food access regardless of how you measure them.

title: Vulnerability Ranking
text:
Key Findings
1. Education and SNAP are the dominant predictors, essentially tied: SNAP participation (r = 0.76) and percent without a high school diploma (r = 0.75) are the two strongest bivariate predictors of obesity. The random forest breaks the tie. Education carries an importance weight of 0.527, more than double SNAP at 0.241. Both variables concentrate in the same urban core tracts.
2. High educational disadvantage with low obesity is rare and geographically explained: Only two tracts (7.00 and 10.02) have percent without a high school diploma above 10% and obesity below 35%. Tract 7.00 sits east of UNL where a student-adjacent population suppresses obesity despite real food insecurity. Tract 10.02 is primarily commercial with a small residential population that does not carry the financial barriers typical of educational disadvantage. Both are geographic edge cases rather than true exceptions to the pattern.
3. Near grocery tracts have the highest average obesity: Tracts within 1 km of a grocery store average 36.4% obesity, higher than moderate (33.7%) or far access (34.0%) tracts. Urban low-income tracts cluster near stores, but structural poverty drives food insecurity regardless of physical distance.
4. Poverty quartile analysis confirms a monotonic gradient: Average obesity declines consistently from Q1 (37.3%) to Q4 (32.8%). Poverty is a stronger structural driver of health outcomes than grocery distance alone.

title: About
text:
About
I started as a math major at UNL, but kept finding myself drawn to the messier, real world side of problems where the data is imperfect and the answer actually matters to someone. That’s what pulled me toward data science.
Most of my experience has been in data validation and analysis. I built SQL workflows at a Berkshire Hathaway insurance company, managed course evaluation datasets for UNL, and modeled health outcomes at the census tract level using socioeconomic and geographic data. I like work that combines careful methodology and practical impact.
Lately I’ve been getting more interested in bioinformatics. Applying ML and statistical modeling to biological data feels like a natural extension of the kind of work I already do, and it’s a space where rigor really matters. I don’t have a deep biology background yet, but working alongside biology and bioinformatics majors and completing a hands on entomology lab has pushed me in that direction.
Outside of work, I spent a semester studying in Nishinomiya, Japan, and I’m a few years into studying Japanese, mostly for personal reasons, though I suspect it’ll come in handy eventually.
I’m currently looking for data science or analyst roles, with a particular interest in biotech, health, or research adjacent environments.

title: Health Outcomes and Social Determinants in Lancaster County, Nebraska
text:
This analysis extends a class project from Math in the City (Spring 2026), which found that educational attainment was a stronger predictor of obesity in Lancaster County than physical proximity to grocery stores. That project used a limited feature set. Here I add SNAP participation rates and age distribution variables from the ACS to test whether food insecurity changes the picture. It does.

title: Health Outcomes and Social Determinants in Lancaster County, Nebraska
text:
Education and Obesity
Percent of adults without a high school diploma has a bivariate r of 0.75 with obesity prevalence, nearly identical to SNAP participation (r = 0.76). In the random forest, it ranks as the top feature by importance (0.527), well ahead of SNAP (0.241). The OLS model below examines this relationship in detail with a 95% confidence band.

x = df["percent_no_hs"].dropna()
y = df.loc[x.index, "OBESITY_CrudePrev"]

model = sm.OLS(y, sm.add_constant(x)).fit()

ax.scatter(x, y, alpha=0.7, s=50, label="Census tracts")
ax.plot(x_line, pred["mean"], linewidth=2, label="OLS fit")

                alpha=0.2, label="95% CI")

        transform=ax.transAxes, va="top",

ax.set_ylabel("Obesity Prevalence (%)")
ax.set_title("Education and Obesity in Lancaster County")
ax.legend()

text:
Predictive Modeling
We compare a linear regression baseline against a Random Forest regressor. Features are standardized before modeling. The dataset has 78 tracts. Cross validation variance is high, so treat R² values as directional rather than precise.

TARGET = "OBESITY_CrudePrev"

FEATURES = [
    "percent_uninsured",
    "snap_rate",
    "fast_food_density",
    "dist_to_grocery_km",
    "poverty_rate",
    "percent_no_car",
    "percent_no_hs",
    "pct_under_18",
    "pct_65_plus",
]

data = df[FEATURES + [TARGET]].dropna()
X_raw = data[FEATURES]
y = data[TARGET]

scaler = StandardScaler()
X = scaler.fit_transform(X_raw)
y_std = (y - y.mean()) / y.std()

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y_std, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)
print(f"Train: {len(X_train)} tracts | Test: {len(X_test)} tracts")

Train: 62 tracts | Test: 16 tracts



# Linear Regression
lr = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)
y_pred_lr = lr.predict(X_test)

print("Linear Regression")
print(f"  R²   = {r2_score(y_test, y_pred_lr):.3f}")
print(f"  RMSE = {np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, y_pred_lr)):.3f} (standardized units)")

coef_df = (
    pd.DataFrame({"feature": FEATURES, "coefficient": lr.coef_})
    .sort_values("coefficient", key=abs, ascending=False)
)
print()
print(coef_df.to_string(index=False))

Linear Regression
  R²   = 0.517
  RMSE = 0.641 (standardized units)

 percent_uninsured     0.148340

dist_to_grocery_km     0.063998

    percent_no_car     0.020444
 fast_food_density     0.012061


A note on multicollinearity. Several predictors in this model correlate with each other. The most notable pairs are snap_rate and percent_no_hs (r = 0.71), and snap_rate and poverty_rate (r = 0.57). In a linear regression, correlated predictors inflate coefficient variance and make individual estimates unreliable. Read the LR results as directional rather than precise. The model confirms that socioeconomic variables collectively explain meaningful variance, but individual coefficient magnitudes are not reliable guides to predictor importance. The random forest importance scores are less sensitive to correlated features and give a more reliable ranking.

# Random Forest

rf.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_pred_rf = rf.predict(X_test)

print("Random Forest")

print(f"  RMSE = {np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, y_pred_rf)):.3f}")

    pd.DataFrame({"feature": FEATURES, "importance": rf.feature_importances_})
    .sort_values("importance", ascending=False)

title: Health Outcomes and Social Determinants in Lancaster County, Nebraska
text:
Findings and Takeaways
This analysis extended the original Lancaster County health study by adding SNAP participation rates and age distribution variables from the ACS (2024 5-year estimates). The results shift the story from the class project in two ways.
SNAP participation and educational attainment are the two dominant bivariate predictors of obesity, with r = 0.76 and r = 0.75 respectively. They are essentially tied. The random forest breaks this tie differently from the raw correlations. percent_no_hs carries an importance weight of 0.527, more than double snap_rate at 0.241. This reflects their high collinearity (r = 0.71). In an ensemble method, whichever feature captures variance the other does not tends to absorb more importance. The decision tree root split also falls on educational attainment, reinforcing the RF result.
Age distribution added modest but meaningful signal. Tracts with higher shares of residents 65 and older show lower obesity (r = -0.45) but higher coronary heart disease (r = 0.74). That pattern makes biological sense and suggests the three health outcomes have partially distinct drivers. Percent under 18 contributed more through interaction effects than raw correlation, showing up third in random forest importance despite a weak bivariate r of 0.14.
Food access geography stayed the weakest predictor across all methods. Distance to grocery stores (r = -0.17, importance = 0.027) underperformed every socioeconomic variable tested.
The policy picture is more complex than the original analysis suggested. Educational attainment leads the random forest but changes slowly. SNAP participation is a program that can be expanded, made more accessible, and targeted at specific tracts. The concentration of high SNAP rates and low educational attainment in the same urban core neighborhoods shown in the spatial maps points to a clear target. Outreach and enrollment support for SNAP in those areas is the most direct short-term lever available.
Future work could add SNAP enrollment barriers such as application complexity and language access, school meal participation rates, and individual level data to test whether these tract level patterns hold at finer resolution.

After completing the class project, I wanted to test whether adding more policy relevant variables would change the findings. The original analysis identified educational attainment as the strongest predictor of obesity. Adding SNAP participation rates and age distribution data from the ACS shifted that picture considerably.
Key finding. SNAP participation (r = 0.76) and educational attainment (r = 0.75) emerged as essentially tied bivariate predictors of obesity. The random forest breaks the tie. Education leads with an importance weight of 0.527, more than double SNAP at 0.241. The high collinearity between the two (r = 0.71) explains this. Both variables point to the same urban core tracts as the highest risk areas.
Tools. Python, pandas, scikit-learn, geopandas, statsmodels
Data. ACS 5-year 2024, CDC PLACES 2025, OpenStreetMap, TIGER/Line 2020

Added SNAP participation rate, percent population under 18, and percent 65+ from ACS to the original feature set
Random forest feature importance: percent_no_hs (0.527), snap_rate (0.241), pct_under_18 (0.063). Food access variables combined below 0.05.
Linear regression R² = 0.517. Random Forest R² = 0.609 on the held out test set. Repeated K fold CV mean R² = 0.565 (RF) vs 0.299 (LR).
Spatial mapping shows SNAP concentration and low educational attainment overlap almost perfectly in Lancaster County’s urban core
Decision tree (max depth 4) confirmed educational attainment as the primary splitting variable
The age split is notable. pct_65_plus negatively correlates with obesity (r = -0.45) but positively with coronary heart disease (r = 0.74), suggesting distinct drivers across outcomes.






The Lancaster County health analyses produced Python notebooks and reports. This project rebuilds the same dataset as a normalized SQL database to answer the same questions from a different angle. Using DuckDB locally, the data splits into four domain tables and five analytical queries explore poverty, food access, and health outcomes at the census tract level.
Key finding: Near grocery tracts average the highest obesity (36.4%), higher than moderate or far access tracts. The poverty quartile analysis shows average obesity falling consistently from Q1 (37.3%) to Q4 (33.1%). Both findings point to the same conclusion. Structural poverty predicts health outcomes more reliably than physical distance to food.
Tools: Python, DuckDB, pandas, matplotlib Data: ACS 5-year 2024, CDC PLACES 2025
View Notebook


See technical details


Designed a normalized four-table schema (tract_demographics, tract_health, tract_food_access, tract_snap) using DuckDB’s read_csv_auto
Query 01: composite vulnerability score weighted across education (40%), poverty (30%), and SNAP (30%) reflecting random forest importance ordering
Query 02: education outlier query filtering tracts with high educational disadvantage but unexpectedly low obesity; both outliers have geographic explanations tied to UNL proximity and commercial land use
Query 03: CASE-based food access tiers comparing average obesity, poverty, and SNAP rates across near, moderate, and far grocery access groups
Query 04: income vs health outcome comparison using top and bottom 10 income tracts via a RANK() OVER (ORDER BY) window function
Query 05: NTILE(4) to assign poverty quartiles, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY) to rank tracts within each quartile by obesity, and AVG() OVER (PARTITION BY) to compute quartile level averages, all in a single CTE
